questions.q: What happens when a promise behind an await rejects?
options: The function silently returns undefined
It is thrown as a normal, catchable exception right at that await line
The program immediately exits with no message
It automatically retries the operation
questions.explain: A rejection behind await surfaces as a regular thrown exception, which ordinary try/catch can handle like any other error.

questions.q: What is the standard way to handle a rejected await inside an async function?
options: Wrap the await in a try/catch block
Add a .then() after the await
Use a for loop to retry automatically
Rejections inside await cannot be handled
questions.explain: try/catch around an await catches the thrown rejection exactly like it would catch any other synchronous exception.

questions.q: What happens in modern Node.js if an async function's rejected promise has no try/catch and no .catch() anywhere?
options: Nothing — it's automatically ignored
It logs a harmless warning and continues
It becomes an unhandled promise rejection, which crashes the process
It gets automatically retried
questions.explain: Modern Node.js treats unhandled promise rejections as fatal, crashing the process rather than silently continuing.

questions.q: Besides try/catch inside the function, what's another valid way to handle an async function's rejection?
options: Chain .catch() onto the call, since an async function always returns a Promise
There is no other valid way
Wrap the function call in a setTimeout
Use the delete operator on the rejected value
questions.explain: Since async functions always return Promises, calling .catch() on the call site works just as well as try/catch inside the function body.

questions.q: Why is an empty catch block (catch (err) {}) considered a bad habit?
options: It causes a syntax error
It silently swallows the error instead of fixing it, hiding the real bug until it resurfaces elsewhere
It automatically re-throws the error anyway
JavaScript doesn't allow empty catch blocks
questions.explain: Swallowing an error without logging or handling it doesn't eliminate the underlying problem — it just makes it harder to find later.
